blocks.x: I'm B. Steckler.
Yes. And what is your middle name? Is that B? B. Batiste. Batiste. And your name is Bat? Is that right? What? Do they call you Bat? Is that a nickname?
Yeah, that's a nickname, yeah. I was named that French uncle of mine, you know. He emigrated from France here. Oh, yes. And he married my mother's sister, you see.
Yes.
And of course, when I came to the world, he stood Godfather for me. And consequently, he first made that, you see, John Batiste.
Was he a musician, too?
Sir?
Was he a musician? Did he play? No, no, he was no musician. Did your father, mother, anyone play music? No, no. We didn't get your age. When is your birthday? When were you born?
Oh, yeah, on the 22nd of November, 1877. Yes. Understand?
Yes. Where were you born, Mr. Stack?
Right here in New Orleans, downtown, though, in the Ninth Ward. Ah. Does this record what I said?
Yes. We'll have it down on tape, so we'll be able to hear it then, and we can copy it down later on the paper, too. Ah.
Well, just, you can just ask me now, whatever you want to tell me, want me to ask.
I was wondering about the very first music you heard when you were a boy. What kind of music did you hear when you were a boy?

Well, there was a bunch of boys. They wanted to start a brass band, and they asked me about would I get in it. I said, well, yes, if you're going to study music. So I said, well, how are you going to do? You're going to have a professor to, so we got a professor by the name of Joe Telesco. Understand? Yeah. He was a Spanish man, but he was a first-class musician, and he had, I believe, 15 men that started, and whenever he first started this, he started, we'd play eight bars of a piece that was written, you understand? And if anyone made a mistake, he'd stop you, and he'd tell you who made the mistake, and he'd blow it on his clarinet, you see, and tell him, you see, now this is how that goes. And he'd blow it, you understand, all that, and he'd make him rehearse that until he got it down on his horn, you understand? So then we'd go ahead and play the next eight bars, and if that was okay, well, then it would be all right, and then the next eight bars, and so on. And then when all hands had it down pretty pat, well, he'd start them all off, you see, that is the whole band. Well, if anyone, which often happened, if anyone made a mistake, he'd detect it, and he'd stop you, and he'd point to you and say, well, you see, you made a mistake, and he'd blow it. You understand? Now I'm only using my name for that, to give you an illustration, you understand, of how he acted with us. So, we was playing one year, and he said, how would you boys like to play on the carnival parades? So, they all agreed, they thought it was all right, so I agreed, too. I played the carnival parade, but I really couldn't tell you what was the first year we played. You understand?
About how old were you when you had that band?
Well, I was born in 1877, and about 21 years, 19 years, to be exact, when I started fooling around music. But I was quick, I was learning very, very fast.
Did you have any lessons before you joined the band?
No, no, never did. None of us, none of them, had any, any talent about music. They were all greenhorns, and this professor made musicians out of the whole gang of us.
What was your first instrument that you took up? Did you start? Cornet. You started right on cornet.

Yes, sir. And I made a crackerjack, if I have to say it myself. I'm not given to post him, but I'm telling you what's a fact. And so, we had, we, we used to rehearse in my daddy's kitchen. He had a very big kitchen, you know, it was, I believe, 20 feet long, by 16 or 18 feet wide. Now, he says, during the winter months, he says, that's where you all live. So he decided to make a big kitchen, you see. And that's where we used to rehearse, at mine, at 3817 Dauphine Street, in my daddy's home. And he used to get a kick out of that, you understand? And he felt that, he was proud to see young fellas, you know, that wanted to take up something like that. So, alright. So the first thing you know, the ancient order of Harbournia is, at the church down there, the St. Vincent de Paul's church, they had a, they used to have a celebration, you understand? So we told Mr. Terlesco, the professor, we told him about it. So he said, well, we're going to get some music, some pieces, that'll answer the purpose for that. So then on the day, I forget just what day they celebrate that, the ancient order of Harbournia, the church day. You understand? So we were rehearsing pieces and we played for them for nothing. You understand? We didn't want anything for it. We were sort of proud to think that we could do something like that. So we played, that was our first offense, plan for the Harbournia, ancient order of Harbournia. So, well, as times went on, then the carnival come along. And Joe Terlesco says, you fellas like to walk plenty? He says, I'll get you a job, plan for the carnival parade. So, alright. The American Brass Band, that's what we named it. And we came along and we, we done very well. So as times went on, some fellas got mad and understand, and he's kind of drifted apart. So when I got married, I, I didn't bother so much with, the only, sometimes fellas would come to me and ask me, didn't I want to go out a while tonight and serenade fellas. So I told him, I said, well, I'll tell you, I don't mind going with you. But I said, I got a time limit. I told him, when 11 o'clock comes, I'm going. I ain't fooling no longer because I'm, I got a wife. And I was learning to trade brick work instead with my daddy. He was a crackerjack brickler. And he made a good one out of me too. Let me, let me tell you that. I didn't borrow no man. I'd milk, I'd milk, everything was known, made out of bricks. I made canning kittles. I made kittles for the, for the butchers to make sausage, cooked sausage in. You understand? They don't have that no more. They had cooked sausage in and a smoke house with a hole in the front where the smoke would be in there. Just one little hole about that square. You understand? Three or four inches square where the smoke could come out. And they used to hang the sausage up there and there on sticks and smoke them. So, oh I, then later on in years, I, I got to, I made a, a copron under Father Prim's church. You understand? He was so well pleased to see that. I was recommended by a man who, that I know my onions. So, he was so well pleased the way I had made that so nice and round. You see, I drawed the, with a, a cornish. I made the, I made the, I made the form and then I set the rails and I drawed that perfect. So he says to me, you a mighty good man at this. I said, yes sir. He says, well, he says, I'm going to see Gunter and I'm going to make Gunter go and see you about building some copons in, in the cemetery. So, when I did go, I told him, I said, I wouldn't build one at a time because I said, I got my brother who works with me. And I said, he's just as good a mechanic as I am. And I said, when I'd be laying bricks, he could be cementing. Or if he'd be laying bricks, I could be drawing a cornish and on them posts and so on. Well, I wouldn't make but five at a time. But I'd done everything that was known to be in line of brickwork. Everything. I built four flue chimneys, I built eight flue chimneys, I built six flue chimneys. I built everything. Then, once I got slack, I used to go work for the Southern Railroad Company. A fellow that knew me, Lacey, he used to work regularly. And he saw me one day and he said, you ain't working? I said, not right now. He said, well, you want to go to work? He said, I can get you done with J.C. Hall, the resident engineer. I said, well, all right. He said, go down and see him. He said, you can see him there pressing the river. And he says, he'll entertain you. So he asked me whether I was a first class man. I said, well, I said, you'll have to ask Mr. Lacey about that. I said, I worked with him. And I said, I never had a wrong word with him. And I said, everything he told me to do, I'd done it to his satisfaction. So he said, well, all right, I'm going to give you a pass now. And he says, tomorrow morning, you're catching number six out of here and you're going up to Lacey. And he was putting up a tank formation then. And from there I went to all the way to Meridian.
Well, I was wondering some more about this American brass band.
We're in it. We're still up, eh?
How many people were in there? How many musicians did you have? Ten. Ten?
Ten. Sometimes 12. It depended on how the people that wanted to hire. They said, well, I want 12, about 12 men.
Tell us how many cornets, how many trombones and so on.
Well, there was always three cornets players. Three. And sometimes a clarinet player. You see?
Did they use E flat or B flat?

Well, very seldom. E flat cornet is more louder. You understand? They use that more in brass bands that you want to hear it. Now, as a rule, they take an E flat cornet and put that in a concert band. You can hear that damn cornet above all of them. Yeah. It's got a louder tone. But as a rule, we used to use all B flat cornet.
I wondered about the clarinet, too. Was that an E flat, a little short one?
No, no.
Big.

You see, the fellow that I used to often come in contact with is Yellow Nunez. I was telling you about him. He's the first man I ever heard playing jazz. You understand? The way the fellows used to get him. And they'd get me because they knew I was good. And they'd go play over here at the Beater's place on music and play ball. And they'd play all around. You understand?
What kind of a place was that? Just a tavern, bar room?
Yeah, Mr. Peter was a friend of mine. And in the yard, the Beater's social club. Johnny Corsier used to be a barber. And he used to come back there at a dance once in a while. We'd be playing.
They had dancing in that day, you see? They had dancing there.

And they'd dance, you understand? So they formed a club. And we gave two or three dances. And they made enough money to make a platform in the yard with a roof over it. And we profited by it afterwards, though. Because different people used to rent it. And they'd hire us to play. You understand? And they'd have a big time down there.
That was the dance band that played over there?
Yeah. I used to play with string bands and play with brass bands.
That's good. How many instruments in the string bands? What instruments did they have in the string bands?

Well, there's a rule that had violin, guitar, and bass, and clarinet, and sometimes cornet. And sometimes they didn't have no clarinet because they'd much rather have a cornet player. That is, the fellas that used to lead or take the jobs. I know fellas that used to take the jobs. If they only had two stringers, two, what do you call, blowing instruments, they'd sooner have the cornet than the clarinet. But if circumstances or the cases sometimes, well, then they'd have clarinet and cornet.
Did they use trombone much?
Yeah. They used to use trombone, but then not so much.
What about drums? Did they have drums in the string band?
Sometimes. Not at no dances. Except if you go to some of them balls and so on. Well, then you had to have, but these small dances that they had, they never had no drums in that.
In this brass band again, you say three cornets and clarinet, how many trombones? Well, one.

One? One. Just one. Now, of course, they had valve trombone or sliding trombone, and they had valve trombone. Now, Mr. Mallow from down below, his brother used to be a valve trombone player. But he was good, but he never read nothing. But he had a good ear. You could take that fella and you played a piece once, and the next time you played it, he had a down pat, and he could come right in there with his trombone parts, mighty good. But the best trombone player that I ever heard was a fella by the name of Ricky Tom. You understand? Yeah. He come down here with a circus, and he liked it so much down here, and getting around, getting beer around Exchange Alley by Morton's. You could go there and fill up. You understand? They could get free lunch, and you could go in there and buy beer, and if you was hungry, you could get a big sandwich. And if you could get된 stuff with stuff

get another beer and get another sandwich because I know fellas wake up in that section. Not only ponds, but fellas wake up that way and they used to go there and get their lunch and drink beer with their lunch for ten cents and have all they want to eat. Of course those days have gone by forever.
Well, I was like, the living is cheap. He's been everything almost for nothing.

Did Ricky Tom stay here until he died? Do you know? Well, I really couldn't answer that, but he was here a long time. And he played here? Yeah, he played here. And everybody that knew him or he played with anybody, they'd always come back and hire him again. Understand? Now, Exchange Alley, most all of them concert bands that used to play out at the West End. You see, they used to have Palletti's band, well they would rehearse in Exchange Alley. Understand? And Finney's band, they rehearse there in Exchange Alley. But then they used to have out there at West End, you'd be surprised to see the people used to go out there listening to them people play.

I've heard about that. How big a band were those concert bands? Well, they'd run around 50 musicians. 50? Yes, sir. Yeah, 50 men. But they were all good musicians, you see. Every Sunday evening they had a concert then? So? On concerts on every Sunday evening? No, it was on Saturday. Saturday.

Saturday. And I'll tell you, it used to be crowded out there. But today, I don't know, they, they, most of the parties today I believe, you gotta, if you go, they gotta advance maybe around the battle house. And they have a room there where you have your party together. You gotta have booze in your pocket, you see. And get soft drinks. And that's the way most dances is today.
Do you remember the names of some of the people who played with you in that American brass band?

Louis Neasel, Tony Varenholtz. Yeah, he's got the names. Louis Neasel, Tony Varenholtz. Yeah. What's the big play? Well, uh, Tony Varenholtz, he used to play tuba, bass. And Pat Neasel, he used to play, uh, baritone. And, uh, Frank Murrath, he used to play alto. That's a complement instrument, you see. And, uh, let's see. Eddie Falk, he used to be clarinet player. What's his name? Eddie Falk, F-A-L-K. Ah. He used to play trombone, uh, at least clarinet.

Did your teacher, did your teacher ever play with you in that band? Who? Your teacher, the Spanish clarinet player, did he ever play with you in the American? No, he never did play with you. He never did play with you, though.
But he made it, he made sure. He said, if you only played three pieces, he says, I want to see that you're playing right. You understand? And, uh, he used to take something that wasn't so difficult.
Do you remember some of the pieces you played? Well, I remember which numbers.
No, I never did. I never did pay much attention to the, to the pieces that was played.
Were they marches or waltzes or what kind of pieces? Well, yeah, you know. All the ones.
You take in, in the time that I used to go to dances, I used to play at dances.
Well, that's what he wants to know. What pieces you played?

What kind? We used to play waltz first, then polka, then a mazooka, and then a shardish, and then a square dance. We had to be alliances. Yes. Then you'd come back, waltz, polka, mazooka, shardish, and a variety. That's two square dances. You understand? Yes. And then when the next square dance time would come, it'd be a little lances again, you see, and then the next time, variety. That was good times then.
And sometimes, sometimes the middle of the night, when you come, because that time the ball just did all night. That play a Virginia reel. That come in. That was good.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
Did you ever play any more or less things like popular music of today? That is, it would sound anything more ragtime, you might say. Did you play much ragtime in your dance?

No, no. In our time, they never played that. The only man, like I told you before, that I heard putting the police band, got this fellow, Yellow Nunez, and I tell you, he couldn't read nothing, but he could, the minute he'd hear a piece, he could play it as good as you, you would notice. He had a good air. So the fire department, at least the police department, heard of Yellow Nunez, and the first thing you know, he had a uniform on, the police would have been a police band, Yellow Nunez. But he was, he's the first man Al Hoyt blow jazz. And I'm willing to better all that, he was the foundation of jazz music. Because you take them nightclubs, like Al Hoyt and them fellas playing up in Boy Born Street there. All that stuff there, they playing is mostly all jazz stuff. Because I never did see no piece written, no written jazz music. All that jazz is

stuff that they put in. It's not written. Now you said, you told me the other day that you played straight, but you played straight lead, but when the guys that you played with would sort of take off. Is that what you told me the other day? What's that about? You played, you said that you played the straight melody. Yeah, all the time. Right? But the guys that you were playing with might take off or play extra things.

Well, you see, the violin players rule, most all of them that I know that I used to play with, they used to play the melody, you understand, just the same as mostly I would. But they learned all that from me, you see. And that was why every time they'd get a job, they'd come, sometimes they'd be three or four fellas that'd come from me for the play the same night that I had already been engaged. You understand? Yes. Well, the reason they'd done it is just like lances and varieties. Them fellas couldn't play no lances or varieties, but I used to have that in written form. And I used to play the lances and varieties, all true. Well, of course, they used to follow. Well, eventually, with them playing, me playing the melody, they eventually picked up and learned how to play it too, you see. But they didn't in the very beginning. But they was wise enough, you understand, to get a hold of somebody that did know.

Yeah. I was wondering about Gala Nunez. Do you remember about how old he was? Was he older than you? Well, he was a much younger man than I was. Well, he's younger than you. Now, do you know what part of town he came from? Since he's not here, we'll never be able to talk to him and find out. He was a whole

lot younger man than I was. I couldn't tell you his age, but I do know that he was a much younger man than I was. Did he come from about the same part of town, downtown here? Yes. Well, I know somewhere between the Leeson Field and, say, El Manasio over here. Well, what they call it now, they changed the name to Franklin Avenue. Franklin Avenue. Franklin Avenue. And then it runs back from the, way up from the beginning near the river to back here where the, where Franklin Avenue turns off this way. Yeah. And the continuation of the Lafayette Avenue is back there.
Uh, you played, you played with Johnny Schenk. Yeah. Is that right? Yeah. Well, what did the men, who were the men in that beside you, Mr. Stackler? Who played in that beside you?

With Johnny Schenk. Well, Johnny Schenk. Well, nine times out of ten, the fellow John Deveread, uh, John Deveread, he used to play bass with him. And Johnny Williamson, he used to play guitar with him. Uh-huh. And he used to play violin. And then I'd play corners with him, you see? Uh-huh. But, uh, to tell you the truth, now, for a fellow keeping time with a bass fiddle, you understand? Playing dance music, or two-fourth time, or three-fourth time, any time, or six-eighth time, he was the best man that I ever heard play a bass fiddle, and don't let the band run away. You understand? Uh-huh. He'd keep that time up from the start to finish. No running away, like some bands do, you know? Yeah. They start in the proper time, two-fourth time, and the first thing you know, man, they're going in six-eighth time. Well, but John Deveread, him as a bass player, he never did, he never did, uh, go to work and, and run away with, uh, he'd, he'd hold his time, and of course that would bring the, the fellas, the, the melody gang, back to the, to, to the original time. Uh-huh. Do you remember a fellow named Albert Bix? Albert Six? No, Bix, I believe. Maybe Six. Albert Six. Is that it? S-I-X, Six, yeah. Albert Six. Yeah, now let's see, I, I, I remember him and played with him. But, I think he used to play, uh, bass too. Bass fiddle. Yeah. You see? Well, uh, he was, used to play with the string bunch. Uh-huh. All the time. And, uh, that was a fella, he was a joymin' boy, but they, I used to say some of the people when we were playing at a dance, I'd say, get, get two or three drinks in that fella there, and ask him to recite that recitation about Mr. Messina and Mr. Messona. And I'd be damned if that fella couldn't imitate a Dago better than any man I ever heard in my whole life. And he'd start off about the baseball game. About a, they call it a, strike. And he says, he never moved his stick. And he'd give the illustrations, you know, didn't I? And, uh, yeah, he could get, go that mighty good. I used to enjoy that every time I'd be, my, oh, you, used to want to hear. He could imitate a Dago. I, I mean.

What do you mean? Uh, you remember a place called Thoman's Hall or Thoman's Hall? Thoman's Hall on Dauphin between Elmire and Dithaugh. And that was called something else, I believe. Did they call that something else? A different-
The wigwam, wasn't it? Huh? The wigwam, wasn't it? Yeah, I mean, so, it was Thoman's Hall. Thoman's Hall was on the lakeside of Dauphin Street. Uh-huh.

And it was a dance hall? Yeah, they used to rent it out. How about the Rifle Club? Huh? You ever work at a place called the Rifle Club? Well, that is a volunteer rifle club on Ramport near, uh, Montague Street. Uh-huh.
They used to shoot rifle there. And they had a fine floor in there, you see. And the volunteer rifle club used to give dances, you see. And-
Didn't they have one on the Clavin Street too? Huh? Yeah, didn't they have one up on the-
Yeah, there was one up there. The Unexpected Rifle Club.
Unexpected, yeah. Oh, yeah. Unexpected.
Unexpected. On Clayborne between Mandible and Maroney, I think it was. I'm not sure about Mandible and Maroney. That's it.
Ain't it, wasn't it? Yeah, Mandible and Maroney on the one side. Yeah. The lake side.
Now, if there's any other questions that you know and I know anything about them, I'll short answer them.

I wanted to ask about a few of the parks. We'll ask you in a minute about Millenburg too. But I have a name, some names of some real old parks here. The Crescent Pleasure Park. Do you remember that? Crescent Pleasure Park. It said it was next to the Oakland Park, which was out at the near Metry Road, on the Shell Road. Do you remember Oakland? No. Riding Park. That was the riding park. No, I don't. I don't know if they had races or what they had there. No, I don't know nothing about that. That must have been up in Jefferson Parish. Yes, out in Metry, I suppose. Yeah, that's Jefferson Parish. There's a few other parks here I was going to ask. Southern Park. Oh, yes.
Oh, yeah, that was back there. By St. John. Back along by St. John. Southern Park.
Yes, all the picnics and everything out there. So they have music there too?

Oh, yeah, they used to have a regular lay there. Because the gardeners used to give a picnic there. And when the young girls, their daughter would be, you know, sitting down there, and the fellow would come along, he'd top them on the show and tell them, dance with my daughter and I'll give you a quarter. Yeah. To get them to dance with some of them girls. Then they had at the gardeners picnic, they had a fellow every year. He used to win the best prize on tomatoes. You see? Of course, it was open to all the vegetable growers to enter the best that they could raise and show it. And they'd win the prize on them. So this old brother, I can't think of his name anymore. But every year he used to win the first prize on tomatoes. So I was doing some work down near his place. And I said to him, his name is Mark.

might come to me later. I said to him, you must have some device that you, or something that you pump in those tomatoes to make them develop so big. I said, can't you tell the fella the name? He says, that's what all of them gardeners is trying to find out. He says, I know I got that laid up every year that I'm going to win the first prize on tomatoes.
Do you remember the names of any of the bands that played out at this Southern Park?

Southern Park? Uh huh. Well, Frobus Band used to play there. Frobus? Frobus. I believe I told you about that. The family pretty near layout. Well, I didn't hear. You didn't tell me about that. The whole family played? Well, you see that the older folks got married and they had children and they taught them children to play music. And when they did get big enough to play, it was a common thing for them to be playing out at Woodrow Gordon or Washington Gordon for different people that hired bands, you see. And they had a whole Frobus Band and the other one in there was named Frobus. Was it more of a brass band? Brass band. That's what it was, brass band. Where did they live about? Well, they used to live down around Port Street here, between St. Claude and Ramport Street. And of course, some of them spread about in different sections. But the best part of them lived, I'll say, between Almonaster, that's down here at the corner, it used to be. Franklin Avenue now. And Franklin Avenue now. Between there and the sudden railroad track.
Yes. Press Street. Yes. I was going to ask you about a couple more parks. Sportsman's Park. Do you remember that?
Yeah. I remember now. Let's see. Sportsman's Park. I don't think I ever went to anything there, but I, on the door, I know I never played there. But I think that was out on Tulane Avenue.
There's another place, Loper's Park. I think you, I don't know how you pronounce it, Loper's, L-O-E-P-E-R-S, Loper's Park, on Bienville Street.
That must have been back on, near the, near what you call it, but, actually, Road, or what they call that street. Thank you. Thank you.

Okay, it's going again. There's a couple more things I was going to ask about. Way back in the beginning, when you started on Barnett, what kind of an instrument did you get? And where did you get it?

Well, I got a, a Korn instrument. A Korn. G.W. Korn, I think, was the proper initial. I think it's G.W. Korn. And where'd you buy it? I may be mistaken, but it was a Korn instrument. C-O-N-N. Yeah, C.G. Korn. C.G. Well, let's not see. Where'd you get, where'd you buy it? I got that from, well, I think it was.
On Canal Street. Yes, sir. Did your father encourage you to take it up? How come you wanted to take up Korn? Did you like music when you were a boy? Did you hear any bands? I did, yes, sir, I did.
Did you hear any? I'm just going to give you an idea if I like, like music. I used to go to the old lake at a private picnic. And that started in the morning about 10 o'clock.
You were talking about, did you like to play music? No, no, I mean even to hear it, even before. Yeah, that's good.
Yeah. So I used to dance all day. Then they'd always have a dance at Woodrow's Garden and over at Washington Garden, even vice-voisa. They'd never have two at the same Sunday.
What kind of music did they have there?
Grass band.
Grass band. But they played dance music. Dance music.
They all danced. And in them days, you see, it was all the square dances. Yeah. Four, at least waltz, poker, mazzucca, and shardish, and then the square dance.
So they called those quadrilles sometimes too? Quadrilles.

Quadrilles. That's a nigger dance more so than white that I ever know. Quadrilles. I never know nothing. I never did dance no quadrilles. But I danced every other that the white folks danced. So I think it was. A Virginia reel. Huh? And a Virginia reel. Yeah, a Virginia reel. But a quadrille, I think that was a nigger dance.

I've seen some of the music published though up north too, in New York and places, and even in England they called them quadrilles. But I guess they played them in some places here. No doubt. And that was always a brass band at those dances then.
Yeah, all them picnics that they give out there was brass bands.
About ten or twelve pieces or how big would they have?
Yeah, the band would be mostly ten. Ten pieces? And not more than twelve. Uh huh.
And remember whose band that was that you'd go to dance to? Do you remember what the name of the band or who the leader was? Well, uh...
No, I don't. I can't. I know a probus band used to play out there pretty much. Well, you know all about that.
That was before you took up music then, before you played?

Well, no doubt. Yeah. Because I used to go to them private picnics and then I'd go to Ada Woodrow or Washington Garden and I'd dance till midnight and catch Smokey Mary. They used to call that Smokey Mary. That train used to go out there. And the camellia used to land it, which I showed you the picture of it here, alongside the wharf. So if you'd want to make a picture of that, copy it here, where you could do it.
Um, those places were right near the wharf then, Woodrow's? Yeah. That is, right at the edge of the lake. Yeah.
You see where the water started, it was not only a hundred feet away from where this dance provision would be, on both sides of life.
